items.title: Off to Scotland - Happiness, solitude and oysters | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Lars used to be a police officer. Together with his wife Sandy and their young son, he moved from Germany to a remote Scottish island in the Atlantic.

Colonsay has only 120 inhabitants, a shop and a café - and not much else. Lars was keen to escape big city life and pitched the idea to his Scottish wife, Sandy. She agreed to relocate their family and move to Colonsay. The remote island is where she grew up; she and Lars even got married there a few years ago. 
Lars is a lively, sociable type. Will the solitude and almost eerie tranquility on the island in winter suit him? Lars’ father-in-law runs an oyster farm on Colonsay. He’d been looking for someone to take over the business and now Lars is there to help. It’s a tough business. In summer, life feels like a holiday. But in winter, ‘the demons come’, as the islanders say. Lars, too, is struggling with his past. It’s only light for a few hours a day in winter, and the island is often battered by storms. While Sandy starts working from home again, Lars spends a lot of time with their son. He’s also a keen cold-water swimmer. Whenever he can, he ventures into the icy, raging seas that surround the island.

items.title: The Strange Reason Men Used To Dress Like This
items.author: Weird History
items.content:
<article>For centuries, men’s fashion was anything but boring. The wealthiest and most powerful men in history were often the biggest fashion trendsetters and they wore elaborate clothing, extravagant accessories, wigs, makeup, heels, and enough decoration to make modern red carpets look tame. So why did men’s fashion go from flamboyant and extravagant to the relatively restrained suits and casualwear we associate with men today? And why did fashion eventually become so strongly associated with women?

On this episode of Weird History, we look back at a time when high society demanded that men look fashionable, wealthy, and impossibly extravagant to explain how much of the blame can be traced back to one extraordinarily influential man whose choices helped permanently reshape the way an entire gender thought about clothing.

Do you wish more men still dressed with flair? Let us know in the comments.

items.title: Truth under pressure: Life as an investigative journalist in Kyrgyzstan | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>What does it mean to practice investigative journalism in Kyrgyzstan? What are the consequences of holding politicians accountable for corruption? Here, practicing journalism can be life-threatening.

Instead of being celebrated as heroes, journalists in the Central Asian republic of Kyrgyzstan often face threats. Their private lives suffer, as does their safety—and sometimes even their very lives wind up on the line.
Ali Toktakunov, one of Kyrgyzstan’s best-known investigative journalists, stands up to the ruling elite by exposing a corruption case. But when his most important informant is shot dead, Toktakunov flees to the Czech Republic.
The tension between his personal life and his work is brought to light by director Samara Sagynbaeva—who is also his wife. Her diary-style documentary paints a portrait of a courageous journalist. At the same time, the film serves as a reminder of the fragility of democracy and the rule of law in a country where freedom of expression is by no means a given.

items.title: The Social Reckoning That Wasn't
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Go to https://surfshark.com/boyle or use code BOYLE at checkout to get 4 extra months of Surfshark!

Last month Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion dollars to settle claims that it knowingly harmed teenagers — a number the press immediately called Big Tech's "tobacco moment." Wall Street responded by sending the stock up.

In this video I read the actual 130-page consent judgment so that you don't have to, and work out what Meta really bought for its money. It turns out the headline figure is worth about two days of revenue, the "new" safety rules are mostly settings Meta had already written for itself, and the fine print lands rather more heavily on TikTok than on Meta. We'll also get into why the attorneys general took the deal, what Meta was actually paying to make disappear, and why the real reckoning might end up happening in a cinema rather than a courtroom.

items.title: Laughing to survive - On tour with the Palestine Comedy Club | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Six Palestinian comedians go on tour in Israel and the Palestinian territories. What begins as a stand-up comedy show evolves, in the face of terror and war, into a plea for humanity.

Although there are no comedy clubs -- and hardly any stand-up comedy -- in the Palestinian territories, comedian Alaa Shehada decides to found a stand-up comedy troupe, along with other local artists. Their goal? To develop a program that combines Western comedic traditions with Palestinian narrative forms, to perform in front of an audience.

Despite cultural and security hurdles, the group’s six members—each holding a different travel permit—manage to stage a tour of theaters in the Palestinian territories and in Israel. The shows are well attended, and the group begins to gain attention, even internationally.

Eventually, they receive an invitation to London for a series of performances. These are set to begin on, of all days, October 7, 2023. Against the backdrop of Hamas’ terrorist attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, the comedians face the challenge of performing before an increasingly polarized audience in the UK.

Palestine Comedy Club is a film about the search for humor in everyday life under excruciating conditions—and the attempt to forge connections through shared laughter.

items.title: What Does Extreme Heat Do to the Body?
items.author: PBS
items.content:

items.title: San Bernardino Train Crash: What Caused This 100mph Runaway Train?
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>On May 12, 1989, Southern Pacific freight train 7551 rocketed down California’s Cajon Pass at over 100 mph before derailing into a San Bernardino neighborhood. Caused by fatal weight miscalculations and failing brakes, the crash killed four people and destroyed seven homes. But thirteen days later, a second catastrophe struck the exact same street when a damaged underground pipeline ruptured, igniting a massive inferno. This documentary investigates the series of tragic human errors, mechanical failures, and oversight lapses that led to one of the most disastrous chain reactions in American transportation history.

items.title: Black people in Nazi Germany - Lionel Romney's survival in a concentration camp | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Afro-Caribbean sailor Lionel Romney survived eleven months in a concentration camp. His story illustrates how Black people were systematically persecuted under the Nazi regime.

Lionel Romney was born in Santo Domingo in 1912 and raised on Sint Maarten. As a young man, he signed on to a cargo ship to see the world. But his longing for freedom turned into a tragic odyssey. Caught up in the turmoil of World War II, his ship came under fire and sunk. The crew survived. But Lionel was taken prisoner by the Italians. After years in various camps, he was eventually deported to the Mauthausen concentration camp. He survived there for eleven months, before American troops liberated the camp.
Decades after the war, Lionel Romney entrusted his memories to his daughter, Mary. Her journey from the Caribbean through Italy to Austria forms the framework of the film, which shines a light on a chapter of European history that has been suppressed to this day: the reality of life for Black people under National Socialism. This reality was marked by colonial continuities, racism, forced labor, and political arbitrariness. Lionel Romney was one of many who were exploited for propaganda purposes or subjected to persecution.
Experts such as Clarence Lusane, Katharina Oguntoye, Walter Sauer, and Serge Bilé discuss historical perspectives. Archival footage and artistic reenactments weave together, in a rich visual narrative.

items.title: What happens when a blue state votes on trans sports?
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Twenty-seven Republican-controlled states have imposed measures to restrict trans athletes from playing in girls’ and women’s sports since 2020, but this November will be the first time voters have a chance to weigh in on the question directly. Ballot measures are appearing this year in Washington, Arizona, Colorado and Nebraska. 

But Washington’s goes further than any other state in one key way: it would apply to all students seeking to play girls’ sports, not just athletes whose eligibility has been challenged.

The initiative, I-638, would require every girl to prove their sex assigned at birth, via “only one or more of the following: the student's reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.”

Opponents — like Kelsey Gellner, Seattle-based pediatric nurse and board member for the Washington State Nurses Association —  organizing under the NO HATE in WA State campaign, warn that the more than 150,000 school-age girls in Washington without a regular family doctor may be forced to undergo invasive genital inspections, or forgo participation in sports altogether if they can’t afford the alternative testing options.

Supporters — like Dr. Erica Li, a board-certified pediatrician in Spokane, Washington — organizing with Let's Go WA, say the fears are overblown and represent a common-sense and popular reform. Vox’s Rachel Booth talks with organizers and medical providers in Washington about what’s at stake. items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Mental health struggles can be hard to spot, especially among men in workplaces where strength is often associated with staying silent. 

In Ireland, around one in eight male construction workers is affected by depression, and men are almost four times more likely than women to die by suicide. In Germany, the suicide rate is three times higher for men than for women. 

The CAIRDE initiative in Ireland aims to encourage men working in construction to recognize early warning signs, talk openly about mental health issues, and support one another before a crisis develops.

items.title: An Exploration of Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>An intimate and profound investigation of the spiritual aftershocks of the 9/11 attacks. (Aired 2002)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

For many people, the most difficult questions after the deadly terror attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, were not about politics, military strategy, or homeland security. They were questions about God, evil and the potential for darkness within religion itself. And for many, those questions didn’t go away.

In “Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero,” FRONTLINE producer Helen Whitney set out to discover how the religious beliefs of Americans were challenged a year after the attacks. 

From survivors who were pulled from the wreckage of the Twin Towers to the widow of a New York City firefighter; from priests and rabbis to security guards and an opera singer; from lapsed Catholics and Jews to Buddhists, Muslims, and atheists, this documentary explored and illuminated the myriad of spiritual questions that came out of the terror, pain, and destruction at Ground Zero.

“Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero” was a co-production with Helen Whitney Productions. It was written by Helen Whitney and Ron Rosenbaum. It was produced by Helen Whitney. It was reported by Leslie Berger, William Dowell, Lesley Karsten-DiNicola, and Elaine Rivera. The executive editor of FRONTLINE was Louis Wiley Jr. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

In the run-up to the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, we are making a number of seminal documentaries from the days and years after 9/11 available to stream on YouTube for the first time. These documentaries offer a profound historical record of the attacks, what led up to them, the U.S. government's response, and the ripple effects across the U.S. and the world.

<article>Official website: https://to.pbs.org/crimeandpunishment 
Crime and Punishment in America is a four-part series, directed by Lynn Novick, that tells the story of criminal justice in America from the colonial era to today, and explores how for more than 250 years, Americans have wrestled with the problem of crime, the purpose of punishment and the meaning of justice. Executive produced by Ken Burns and Sam Pollard. Narrated by Keith David. 

To address the problem of crime in their new nation, Americans developed a new system of punishment. Instead of being whipped, shamed, or executed in the public square, which was thought of as ineffective and cruel, people who broke the law would be locked away in prisons and penitentiaries, where they were expected to repent, and return to society reformed. 

A sweeping look at the American criminal justice system, from the origins of prisons and policing to our continued fascination with crime, the film traces the contours of our imperfect system and how it influences nearly all parts of our society: the media, economics and politics. Through the voices and testimony of those who have committed crimes, experienced incarceration, enforced the law, or lost loved ones to violence, the series explores the cost of America’s choices and the enduring tension between crime and punishment, vengeance and mercy, justice and redemption.

items.title: All About The New Telescope NASA Just Launched, with Jason Rhodes
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Get the NEW StarTalk book, 'Lost in Space: 5,000 Facts for Navigating the Universe' on Amazon: https://amzn.to/4cCD19e

How do you build a telescope to study something you can't see? Neil deGrasse Tyson and Paul Mecurio sit down with Jason Rhodes, senior research scientist at JPL, to explore the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and its search for answers on dark energy and dark matter.

What is dark energy? Who was Nancy Grace Roman? We explore the story of Nancy Grace Roman herself before diving into why Lagrange Point 2 has become the most valuable piece of real estate in space. When will this special spot in space get too full? The conversation also tackles the growing problem of satellite streaks contaminating observations from both ground and space-based telescopes.

How does Roman actually measure dark energy? Jason walks through three approaches: using Type Ia supernovae as standard candles to measure the universe's accelerating expansion, mapping the clustering of galaxies across cosmic time, and using weak gravitational lensing to trace dark matter by the subtle distortions it imprints on light from distant galaxies. Will this telescope finally put an end to Hubble tension? Could evolving dark energy or modified gravity finally replace Einstein's cosmological constant?

Learn about the two different devices within the Roman telescope: the coronagraph and the wide field. We explore how the coronagraph could enable direct imaging of exoplanets and eventually the search for atmospheric biomarkers like oxygen and methane. We talk about how microlensing could detect rogue planets floating free of any star, which may actually outnumber planets in stable orbits. Plus, how much information can a single pixel bring? More than you’d think!

items.title: Daily life in a German prison | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Around 44,000 men and women are incarcerated in Germany's approximately 170 prisons. About 1,800 are serving time for murder, while most are incarcerated for assault, robbery, theft or drug-related offenses.

One of them is Marcel M., serving time in Berlin's Plötzensee Prison. A repeat offender, he calls it "Stealing, stealing, stealing — all for the addiction." Marcel was living with a drug addiction, it's landed him in prison several times. He's already spent a third of his life behind bars. He wants this to be the last time. Marcel is finishing up his training in the prison's car workshop. After he's released, he wants to find a steady job.
Plötzensee Prison in Berlin has space for around 650 places for male inmates. Some 250 correctional officers look after the prisoners in shifts. Helena Emisch has worked there for eight years now. She knows the prison inside and out and aims each day to strike a balance between professional distance and connecting with the inmates. Locking and unlocking cells, head counts, distributing packages, administering medication and supervising the yard before recreational time are all part of her job. She also conducts cell searches, looking for drugs and other illegal items. "It's a game of cat and mouse between us and the inmates. Sometimes we win, sometimes they do," she says.
Vechta is home to the only women's prison in the German state of Lower Saxony. Melanie F. is one of around 300 inmates there. She, too, turned to crime because of her drug use. She's now serving her third prison sentence — this time for armed robbery. "Prison was hell for me, and prison saved me," she says. Melanie now describes the prison as her substitute family. She feels more at home at Vechta Prison than she does in the outside world. Inside,  she's now completed her drug treatment and is currently training to work as a painter.

items.title: Scientific "unboxing" of a mysterious underwater world
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Down where the light starts to fade — between around 30 and 150 meters below the ocean surface — there are mysterious "mesophotic coral ecosystems," also known as "deep reefs." 

These ecosystems are hard to dive down into, and therefore hard to study, so we still don’t know much about them. Like even what creatures live there.

To learn more, Luiz Rocha, a curator of ichthyology at the California Academy of Sciences, dove down into the depths in Palau, Guam, the Marshall Islands, and French Polynesia between 2016 and 2018 and left behind scientific devices known as ARMS (Autonomous Reef Monitoring Structures).

Those structures spent almost a decade becoming encrusted with deep reef life, slowly turning into mini versions of the reefs themselves. Earlier this year, Rocha and colleagues from several institutions returned to Palau to retrieve the ARMS and unwrap them like scientific presents.

Vox's Byrd Pinkerton, host of the Unexplainable podcast, went along to watch that process. Read her article about it at the link in our bio.

Over 900 gleaming gold coins. A mystery over 2,000 years in the making. What unfolds is a deeply personal chronicle of surviving war, exile and heartbreak, as Israa grows up navigating adolescence, identity and belonging far from the home she was forced to leave. As Israa settles into life in Germany, new freedoms collide with traditions, testing her relationships and reshaping her sense of self.

Co-directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes, the film bears witness to the remarkable trust between filmmakers and family, following Israa and her loved ones across borders, cultures and shifting circumstances. An intimate and nuanced coming-of-age story, ONE IN A MILLION illuminates the complexities of the refugee experience while asking a universal question: what does it truly mean to call a place home?

items.title: Breaking taboos in Italy - Opening an exclusively male ritual to women | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Every year, the Italian town of Viterbo honors its patron saint, Santa Rosa, with a unique procession. A 30-metre-high sculpture has traditionally been carried through the town by more than 100 men. Now, women are challenging that exclusionary custom.

Viterbo is an Italian town with a centuries-old tradition. Every year, on 3 September, more than a hundred men carry the huge Macchina di Santa Rosa sculpture - standing almost 30 meters tall - through the old town. For many, this ritual is a defining part of their identity. But Viterbo is changing, and a new generation is questioning why this tradition is reserved for men.

At the heart of this development is 13-year-old Stella. She was the first girl to be accepted into the Mini-Macchina club - the first step for children hoping to one day become fully-fledged Macchina bearers. Now she's preparing for her most important challenge. For the first time, she's allowed to take part in what's known as the steep stage to the Santuario di Santa Rosa, a symbolic highlight of the ritual.

One of the bearers is Stella's father, David. He is very supportive of his daughter's dream - although it's unusual. Stella's cousin Matteo, on the other hand, sees the tradition from a male perspective. This contrast shows just how deeply rooted gender roles are in Viterbo.

A key figure in this quiet revolution is Gianni Baiocco. Himself a bearer, he is also the chairman of the Mini-Macchina association, located in the town’s historic center. He was one of those who first allowed girls to join two years ago - a bold move that faced some local resistance. As he sees it, this development is about safeguarding tradition, in a sparsely populated area that faces a shortage of young people.

On the day of the Mini-Macchina parade, Viterbo is on the edge of its seat. The film shows just how far Stella's determination and strength will take her. But the question remains as to how far a centuries-old, male-dominated tradition is prepared to open up. This is a report on courage, cultural heritage and the transformation of a city caught between faith, tradition and a new generation.

items.title: Afghanistan: Negotiating with the Taliban | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Before the Taliban’s return, a brief hope was ignited. Could Afghanistan become a more just country? A group of Afghan women sat at the negotiating table. But after the Taliban took power in 2021, those dreams were dashed.

Four women were part of an Afghan negotiating team that included representatives of the former government. They wrestled with the Taliban over the future of Afghanistan. Although it was life-threatening for them to raise their voices against the Taliban's misogynistic regime, they never gave up hope of preserving the women of Afghanistan’s hard-won rights. 
The team's intelligence, perseverance and bravery in the face of a hopeless situation are characteristic, when it comes to women around the world who fight for both peace and equality. But the Taliban were not interested in a democratic, free society in which girls and women have basic rights and can go to school, study or work. After decades of war and chaos, Afghanistan has become safer under the Taliban. But the price for women is high: they have paid with their freedom.

items.title: How The Brain Perceives Time, with David Eagleman
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>What are the limits of the human mind? Neil deGrasse Tyson and co-hosts Chuck Nice and Gary O’Reilly turn the telescope inward exploring sensory perception, dreaming, synesthesia, time, and the astonishing flexibility of the human brain with neuroscientist David Eagleman. Why does time seem to slow down during an emergency?

We explore the brain’s flexibility in how it receives and interprets sensory signals. Can you see with your tongue? Eagleman explains how the brain doesn't actually care where information comes from. We explore sensory differences like blind people navigating the world through vibrations on their skin, echolocation, and tactile reading systems like Tadoma, and how the brain repurposes space for what’s needed. 

Could dreams be the visual cortex defending its territory against a takeover from other senses during sleep? Learn about the transitions your brain makes in modulating sensory data. Are dreams the brain's screensaver? We discuss how the more neurologically plastic the species, the more it dreams. Why don't we remember our dreams? Why does eyewitness testimony fail so dramatically? What does the invisible gorilla experiment reveal about how little of reality we actually perceive? We explore how memory isn't a recorder, it's a reconstruction.

Learn about synesthesia, aphantasia, tetrachromacy, and how some of Pixar's best animators turned out to have no visual imagery in their heads at all. We break down time perception and why time seems to slow down in life-threatening situations. David tells us about how he dropped subjects from a 150-foot tower to find out. We explore memory density and why childhood summers felt endless and adult years blur past. Could time perception be the key to understanding and developing treatments for schizophrenia? Plus, the hardest question in all of science: why does it feel like anything to be a brain?

items.title: Our body as a "high-performance machine" - How resilient are we? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The human body is adaptable, resilient, and astonishingly capable — truly a "high-performance machine". Humans have always sought to test their limits. But how resilient are we really?


This film explores the tension between our bodies' impressive capabilities, and the moments when they clearly say 'enough is enough.' How resilient is the human body really? Where are its limits, and what happens when we cross them?
In his youth, Stefan Santifaller tested his physical capabilities so hard as a competitive athlete that he became seriously ill. Pushing physical limits can very quickly push a person to their mental limits as well. When that happened to Stefan Santifaller, it forced him to reorient his life.
Even in everyday life, we can reach our mental limits—whether due to worries in our personal lives or at work. When this type of overload happens, the body sends out signals, or "warning signs." Those affected often feel nervous, restless, depressed, tired, or weak. Sleeping problems, dizziness, muscle tension, anxiety, and mental blocks are possible. Rapid breathing, heart palpitations, or nausea can also follow.
Sometimes, we reach our limits involuntarily, as a stroke of fate bring us to a halt. Markus Rehm experienced this as a young person, when he lost his lower leg in an accident. Today he is a para-long jumper and the newly crowned world champion in his discipline. 
He had to learn the hard way just how definitive physical limits can be, and how much energy — both physical and mental — it takes to chart a new course to circumvent seemingly-insurmountable barriers.

items.title: Argentina's stolen children - The crimes of the military dictatorship | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From March 1976, Argentina was ruled for several years by a military junta led by General Jorge Videla. Some 30,000 people were abducted and murdered by the regime’s security forces. Many of their children disappeared - but where did they go?

Following the military coup in 1976, a systematic campaign of repression began. Around 30,000 Argentinians were abducted and murdered by the security forces - including some 500 women who were pregnant or had recently given birth. For years, no one knew what had happened to the children of these 'disappeared' women.  Had they perished along with their mothers?  Or had they perhaps survived?

After searching for many years, investigators made a shocking discovery: many of these children had been secretly adopted by families with links to the military, and raised under new identities. In some cases, they were living with people who had been involved in the crimes committed against their parents.

The documentary traces the history of Argentina's disappeared children and follows families’ ongoing search for truth, identity and justice. It focuses on the mothers and grandmothers who have been searching for their loved ones for decades, as well as the children themselves, now adults coming to terms with their origins and the circumstances of their past.

ABSTRACT
Building on my 2022 talk, "From Kubernetes to PaaS to... err, what's next," I aim to summarise the core goals of platform engineering to the software developer and architect communities.

My primary goal is for developers to understand "what good looks like" with a successful platform build and help them understand how a platform can influence the SDLC (for better or worse!)

Key takeaways from the session:
• Identify the core goals of a platform from a business and software delivery perspective
• Explore how platform architecture influences software architecture and vice versa
• Learn why the principles of coupling and cohesion apply to platform components (and configuration) in the same way as they do with software components
• Understand what to expect from an effective platform, including the influence on how applications are built, shipped, and run
• Learn about key platform metrics grounded in developer experience frameworks such as DORA, SPACE, and DevEx [...]

items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>How the U.S. government built a huge and hidden anti-terror apparatus after the 9/11 attacks. (Aired 2011)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In “Top Secret America,” Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Dana Priest investigated the growth of a massive maze of clandestine government and private agencies aimed at fighting terrorism after the 9/11 attacks.

Those secret efforts, she and her team reported, included a covert international war waged by the CIA that included drone strikes, black site prisons, and “enhanced interrogation techniques” widely criticized as torture; a domestic surveillance program that authorized the NSA to intercept certain telephone calls and emails of American citizens without a warrant; and other anti-terror programs.

The documentary shed new light on the nature, scale and scope of the government’s counter-terror operations after 9/11 — and explored mounting questions about those programs’ effectiveness. 

“Top Secret America” was directed by Michael Kirk. It was written by Michael Kirk and Mike Wiser, and produced by Michael Kirk, Mike Wiser and Jim Gilmore. It was reported by Dana Priest, Jim Gilmore and William Arkin. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

In the run-up to the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, we are making a number of seminal documentaries from the days and years after 9/11 available to stream on YouTube for the first time. These documentaries offer a profound historical record of the attacks, what led up to them, the U.S. government's response, and the ripple effects across the U.S. and the world.

items.title: It’s A Bug’s Life, We’re Just Living In It, with Jessica Ware
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Go to https://ground.news/startalk to stay fully informed on the latest Space and Science news. Save 40% off through our link for unlimited access to the Vantage plan this month.

Why are bugs so weird? Neil deGrasse Tyson and Negin Farsad sit down with entomologist, Jessica Ware, to dig into the extraordinary world of bugs, insects the size of navel oranges, how they invented flying and so much more. 

What actually is a bug? Learn how the way an insect eats determines whether they are a bug or not. Jessica traces insects back 400 million years to their single common ancestor. Discover how dragonflies were the original flying design for living things. Why are insects so successful on Earth? They predate dinosaurs by hundreds of millions of years, were the first animals to fly, and have had enough time to fill every ecological niche on the planet.

Learn about dragonfly eyes and how their methods for mating impact their vision. What do dragonfly brains actually look like and what can they remember? Would territorial dragonflies have larger brains than non-territorial ones? Do migratory insects develop bigger brains to navigate? Is there a single common ancestor for all insects? We talk about the species unique to New York, cockroaches that only reluctantly share our spaces, and how warming weather will make our future more buggy. What would actually happen if we eliminated mosquitoes entirely? Jessica walks through why wiping out the three most dangerous species would be a net positive for humans, while the things that eat mosquitoes would largely survive. 

The episode closes on the alarming collapse of insect populations worldwide. We break down all the ways that humans impact insects from light pollution disrupting firefly mating, urbanization destroying habitat, and the sobering reality that all life on land came after insects and still depends on them. Plus: what did bed bugs feed on before beds existed, and just how big can an insect actually get?

items.title: Girls make a comeback - What India and China are doing about the women shortage | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>For decades, many families in India and China did not want daughters. Girls were often aborted, killed as infants, abandoned, or sold. But in recent years, things have started to change.

Political decisions aimed at curbing rapid population growth in India and China, together with a widespread preference for boys for economic reasons, have led to a situation where both countries now have more men than women. Again and again, the preference for sons over daughters caused families to resort to radical measures, ranging from sex-selective abortions to infanticide, the abandonment of girls, and, in China, the sale of girls after birth. As early as 1990, Indian economist Amartya Sen, who would later win the Nobel Prize in Economics, warned that more than 100 million women were "missing" in the developing world, and especially in India and China, in the ratio to men. Today, many men in China and India are unable to find wives due to the shortage of women. That is one of the factors that has led to a shift in thinking in both countries—both in politics and society. Educational initiatives, policy measures and the work of activists are all helping to drive forward the change. We hear from people who are facilitating a comeback of girls and who believe that the birth of a girl is a blessing rather than a burden.

items.title: Plato’s infamous Ship of State thought experiment - Michael Vazquez
items.author: TED-Ed
items.content:
<article>Dig into Plato’s infamous Ship of State thought experiment, which explores how democratic societies handle leadership and power.

--

Imagine a ship struggling in an endless storm. Its captain, though strong and commanding, is a terrible navigator. Neither he nor his crew have been trained to sail, yet they tirelessly vie for control through bribery, flattery, and mutiny, and ignore those with real navigation knowledge. This dysfunctional vessel is Plato's Ship of State. Michael Vazquez explores the infamous thought experiment.

<article>During the Cold War, the US military launched a top-secret quest to revolutionize battlefield mobility by putting individual soldiers in the sky. items.title: Higgs Boson: The God Particle
items.author: SEA
items.content:
<article>In 2012, the world’s most advanced science experiment uncovered the signature of the Higgs Boson, the so-called “God Particle” which gives particles their masses. The Higgs was the last of the Standard Model's particles to be verified experimentally. But far from closing the case, it instead opened a new frontier in physics that today embodies everything we still don’t know about nature’s smallest scales. And so in this video, we will wind back the clock more than half a century, to unravel the history and mysteries of the elusive Higgs Boson.

It's official! SEA is now on Spotify! Stream new uploads every week! https://open.spotify.com/show/4xj3bcmXQYWL4g4r5cI8TS

Join my Discord Server: https://discord.com/invite/sea

IMPORTANT: NO AI IS USED IN MY VIDEOS  
Lately there have been a lot of questions about whether this channel uses AI, so I want to be clear and explicit- NO AI IS USED IN THE PRODUCTION OF MY VIDEOS. I am a solo video creator and amateur writer, my voice is my own, and so are my video concepts and animation sequences. My catalogue of videos goes waaaay back to 2018, and I was making videos like this long before the age of generative AI. 

Below you will be able to find where I sourced my visuals (from real software), background music (from real 3rd party artists) and information used to compose the video (CERN resources and other articles). The thumbnail is real artwork and not AI generated. 

And for this project in particular, I actually went to CERN HQ in Switzerland to learn more about the LHC. You can find pictures from my trip below:
https://www.youtube.com/post/Ugkx9uxF3KxdimLG5VXTYHjaas8nJmVzeUAK

It is my mission to keep alive that old style of “infotainment” YouTube video pioneered by the likes of Lemmino, and I try to achieve that it taking my time and trusting my creative instincts. So if you don’t like AI generated content, consider sticking around! Thanks for understanding :D

items.title: Were The Dead Rabbits Really The Most Dangerous Gang In New York?
items.author: Weird History
items.content:
<article>In the mid-1800s, New York City was a battleground and few places were more dangerous than the infamous Five Points where the anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic Bowery Boys were locked in a brutal cycle of violence with one of the city's most feared street gangs: The Dead Rabbits  If you’ve seen Martin Scorsese’s Gangs of New York, you might recognize the Rabbits as the gang Leonardo DiCaprio's character, Amsterdam Vallon, belonged to. That character is fictitious, but the gang itself was all too real... or was it?

In this episode of Weird History, we dive into the Dead Rabbits, Five Points, Gangs of New York, and the brutal history of 19th-century New York City to uncover what life was really like in one of America’s most dangerous neighborhoods and whether the most feared street gang of its era ever really existed.

items.title: How Much Would an AI Crash Destroy?
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>If you’re looking to upgrade your business wardrobe, I can recommend giving Tailor Store a try. Their shirts are made to your measurements, so you can create something that fits both your body and your personal style. My viewers receive 25% off their first order through my link: https://www.tailorstore.com/patrickboyle

Two chip stocks recently drove seventeen percent of the entire global stock market's return in a single month — which tells you just how concentrated the AI trade has become, and how exposed the average investor now is without realising it. In this video we look at how much wealth an AI crash could actually destroy, with estimates from Dean Baker, former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath, and Oliver Wyman running into the tens of trillions of dollars. We cover why the usual places to hide — small caps, value funds, international stocks — are now  packed with AI stocks, what the Bank for International Settlements found when it compared today's buildout to the great railway and dot-com bubbles, and why a technology being real has never been enough to protect the people who overpaid for it. This isn't a crash prediction. It's a look at the downside risk, the illusion of diversification, and why boring, unexciting investing tends to win in the end.

items.title: Operation Show Of Force: The Complete Story Of The Raid In Tunis
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>In 1988, following a deadly attack on a bus near Israel's nuclear facility, Defense Minister Yitzhak Rabin ordered a high-stakes secret mission. Operating 1,500 miles from home, Israel’s elite special forces unit, Sayeret Matkal, alongside Mossad, planned "Operation Show of Force." Disguised as tourists and backed by naval and air support, commandos infiltrated Tunis to target PLO commander Abu Jihad inside his heavily guarded villa. This high-quality historical documentary reveals the intelligence, deceptive tactics, and dramatic execution behind one of the most ambitious special forces operations in modern military history.

items.title: Modern Computer Architecture & Organization • Jim Ledin & Maciej «MJ» Jedrzejewski • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/articles/452

Jim Ledin - President at Ledin Engineering & Author of “Modern Computer Architecture and Organization” @jledin1 
Maciej «MJ» Jedrzejewski - Tech Agnostic Architect & Author of “Master Software Architecture” @learnsoftwarearchitecture 

RESOURCES
Jim
https://www.linkedin.com/in/jimledin
https://x.com/ledin_eng
https://github.com/jledin
https://ledin.com

MJ
https://github.com/meaboutsoftware
https://www.linkedin.com/in/jedrzejewski-maciej
https://www.fractionalarchitect.io

Links
https://youtu.be/wNT2qkusVrA
https://youtu.be/Pv0cfsastFs
https://youtu.be/cI9dfQLTXlU
https://youtu.be/a2DvXnecXVk

DESCRIPTION
Jim Ledin — author of Modern Computer Architecture and Organization, now in its third edition — joins Maciej "MJ" Jedrzejewski to talk through the book's two brand-new chapters on GPUs and large language models, and the specific challenge of writing about hardware that changes faster than a book can ship. Ledin's approach was to focus on durable architectural principles (parallelism, memory bandwidth, tensor processing, and how systems scale from one chip to an entire data center rack) rather than chasing the current state of the art. For the LLM chapter specifically, he chose GPT-2 as the teaching example precisely because it's open-source and small enough to trace by hand — and because, as he explains, the transformer architecture underneath today's frontier models is fundamentally the same structure, just scaled up.

The most concrete takeaway for engineers: the AI buildout's real bottleneck right now isn't compute, it's memory bandwidth — a shift driving high-bandwidth memory production at the expense of consumer RAM, which Ledin illustrates with a blunt data point (a 32GB DDR5 stick that cost $69 a year ago now runs $440). But asked which single chapter would most change how a working developer with no hardware background thinks about their own code, Ledin doesn't point to AI at all — he points to the chapter on pipelining and cache hierarchy, arguing that most of the thousandfold speedup from 1980s PCs to today came from those optimizations, not clock speed, and that writing cache- and pipeline-friendly code is still one of the highest-leverage skills a developer can have.

ABSTRACT
The modern enterprise has evolved in many ways since some of the typical Enterprise Architecture principles and practices emerged.

In this talk, Simon Rohrer will explain how the nature of the modern enterprise means many legacy Enterprise Architecture principles and practices are no longer applicable.

He makes some suggestions on how a modern EA practice can incorporate agile, DevOps, Systems Thinking and socio-technical ways of working at scale to achieve both short term business value, as well as effecting long term technology and organisation transformation - supporting better value, sooner, safer and happier; breaking dependencies rather than managing them.

Simon's experience comes from over 10 years of leading and practicing Modern Enterprise Architecture in large, highly regulated, long-lived organisations with significant legacy technology estates. [...]

items.title: How Former VP Dick Cheney Led the Charge on the War on Terror (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>An investigation into former Vice President Dick Cheney’s role as chief architect of the war on terror — and his internal war with the CIA. (Aired 2006)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In “The Dark Side,” which aired in 2006, FRONTLINE investigated the internal war that was waged between the intelligence community and former Vice President Dick Cheney after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.

Just after the attacks, Cheney told Americans: “A lot of what needs to be done here will have to be done quietly, without any discussion, using sources and methods that are available to our intelligence agencies.”. He warned the public that the government would have to operate on the “dark side.”

This documentary detailed the vice president’s role as the chief architect of the war on terror, and his battle with former Director of Central Intelligence George Tenet for control of the “dark side.” After 9/11, both leaders acted fast to prepare the U.S. for a new kind of war. But soon a debate grew over the goals of the war on terror, and the decision to go to war in Iraq. 

Drawing on more than 40 interviews and thousands of documents, this film provided a step-by-step examination of what happened inside the councils of war at that time. 

Cheney died on Nov. 3, 2025, at age 84. 

“The Dark Side” was written, produced and directed by Michael Kirk. It was produced and reported by Jim Gilmore. The executive editor of FRONTLINE was Louis Wiley, Jr. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning. 

In the run-up to the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, we are making a number of seminal documentaries from the days and years after 9/11 available to stream on YouTube for the first time. Starting with today’s release of “The Dark Side” and continuing every Tuesday until the week of Sept. 11, these documentaries offer a profound historical record of the attacks, what led up to them, the U.S. government's response, and the ripple effects across the U.S. and the world.

items.title: What’s Going On Inside the Sun? With Lika Guhathakurta
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>T-Mobile 5G Home Internet. https://T-Mobile.com/HomeInternet

Get the NEW StarTalk book, 'Lost in Space: 5,000 Facts for Navigating the Universe' on Amazon: https://amzn.to/4cCD19e

What does it look like beneath the surface of the sun? On this episode, Neil deGrasse Tyson and comedian Chuck Nice discuss the heliosphere, the Parker Solar Probe, and solar storms with heliophysicist Lika Guhathakurta.

How do we know what’s going on inside the sun? We break down the techniques heliophysicists use to infer activity beneath the surface. Plus, how much matter has the sun lost since it began the fusion process? Learn how the sun maintains its mass despite all the energy it radiates.

We explore the sounds the sun would make if you could hear it in space. How might that sound differ between large and small stars? Can you see the boiling plasma on the surface of the sun? We discuss the heliosphere, the region outside the sun influenced by the solar wind, and how it protects us from solar radiation. How have NASA spacecraft “punched through” the heliosphere? What was the mission of the Parker Solar Probe, and what is it doing now?

How do coronal mass ejections interact with our atmosphere? Learn about how the sun creates aurora and Neil and Lika’s experiences with solar storms. Could a coronal mass ejection wipe out all electronics on Earth—or in orbit? What would happen if we had another Carrington Event, the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history?

items.title: We Fired the Most Iconic Sniper Rifles (Over Last 100 Years)
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>How has the sniper rifle evolved over the last 100 years? It's time to find out!

Luke Tomes returns to the Royal Armouries to fire some of the most iconic British sniper rifles of the last 100 years. As always, he is joined by Keeper of Firearms & Artillery, Jonathan Ferguson, who talks him through the history, design and development of each rifle, showcasing how British military sniping has evolved from the battlefields of the Second World War to the modern era.

First up is the Lee-Enfield No. 4 Mk. I (T), the dedicated sniper variant of the British Lee-Enfield rifle developed during the Second World War. Chambered in .303 British, the No. 4 Mk. I (T) was selected for its accuracy and fitted with a telescopic sight, transforming the already proven Lee-Enfield into a specialist precision weapon. Used extensively by British and Commonwealth forces, it combined the fast, smooth action of the Lee-Enfield with the precision required for long-range shooting. It established a foundation for British military sniping that would influence specialist rifles for decades to come.

Second is the L42A1, which represented the next major step in the evolution of the British military sniper rifle. Introduced in the 1970s, the L42A1 was developed from the No. 4 Lee-Enfield and converted to fire the 7.62×51mm NATO cartridge, reflecting the wider adoption of the NATO standard. Retaining the familiar Lee-Enfield action while incorporating a new calibre and improved telescopic sighting system, the L42A1 served British forces for several decades. It demonstrated how a proven wartime design could be adapted to meet the demands of the modern battlefield.

Third up is the L96A1, a rifle that marked a dramatic departure from the Lee-Enfield lineage. Developed by Accuracy International and adopted by the British Army in the 1980s, the L96A1 was chambered in 7.62×51mm NATO and built specifically as a modern precision rifle. Its distinctive design, with a rigid chassis and highly adjustable stock, prioritised accuracy, durability and consistency. The L96A1 became one of the defining British sniper rifles of the late 20th century and helped establish Accuracy International as a major name in precision rifle development.

Next is the L115A3, a long-range precision rifle introduced into British service in the 2000s. Also produced by Accuracy International, the L115A3 is chambered in .338 Lapua Magnum, giving it considerably greater effective range than the 7.62mm rifles that preceded it. Designed for extreme long-range precision, it provided British snipers with increased reach and accuracy in demanding operational environments. The rifle became particularly well known through its use in Afghanistan and represents the move towards larger-calibre systems designed to engage targets at exceptional distances.

Last but not least is the L129A1, a semi-automatic designated marksman rifle introduced to British service in response to the demands of modern combat. Chambered in 7.62×51mm NATO, it is based on the AR-10 pattern and provides accurate, rapid follow-up fire at medium and extended ranges. Unlike the bolt-action sniper rifles that preceded it, the L129A1 is designed to give infantry a precision capability while retaining the speed and versatility of a semi-automatic action. Together with the L115A3, it demonstrates how British military precision firepower has evolved to encompass different roles, from traditional long-range sniping to providing accurate fire in support of infantry operations.

Could there be other universes out there? On this episode, Neil deGrasse Tyson and co-hosts Chuck Nice and Gary O’Reilly answer science questions from celebrities like Steven Spielberg, Josh Scherer, Emily Blunt, and more.

Director Steven Spielberg asks about the empty space inside of an atom. We discuss how wide the gap is between the electrons and the nucleus and what keeps them from crashing into each other. How are scientists working to harness quantum tunneling and entanglement?

Producer Bill Prady asks if the multiverse is real. We break down what the universe looked like during the Big Bang. Can you solve the multiverse with math? Josh Scherer of Mythical Kitchen asks what plants Neil thinks need a genetic update. Learn about how humans have been modifying crops throughout history. Plus, Neil explains how we can get kids to eat their vegetables with GMOs.

Actress Riki Lindhome asks about the most misunderstood concept in the universe. Why do so many movies have sound in space? Would you really float around in a spaceship if you weren’t strapped down? Emily Blunt asks if Neil has ever had an alien encounter.

items.title: The Insane US-Japan Currency Bailout
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Level up your note-taking with Plaud NotePro at https://bit.ly/4c9s3bC and use code PBOYLE for 15% off
Amazon: https://amzn.to/4xFP79Q

In July 2026, the US Treasury did something it hadn't done since 1998: it intervened in the currency markets to prop up the Japanese yen — and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a former Soros hedge fund manager, ran the trade in the strangest way possible, selling euros instead of dollars without telling the ECB. But this was never really about Japan. It was about protecting American borrowing costs at a moment when the US is paying more to borrow than it has in decades — with 30-year Treasury yields hitting their highest since 2001. This video breaks down the US-Japan yen intervention, the carry trade, the FIMA facility, and Bessent's huge bet on falling interest rates, and asks the real question underneath it all: is the Treasury Secretary a visionary macro trader, or a cornered man making an enormous gamble with the balance sheet of the United States? A look at currency intervention, the eroding "exorbitant privilege" of the dollar, and why America's cheap borrowing may be coming to an end.

items.title: Inside the Fight Against SARS | Hong Kong: Chasing the Virus (full documentary) | FRONTLINE/World
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>The story of how the SARS outbreak unfolded in the early 2000s — and how researchers sought to combat it. (Aired June 2003)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb 

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate 

The COVID-19 pandemic wasn’t the first time the world experienced an outbreak of a never-before-seen type of coronavirus. In the FRONTLINE/World short documentary “Hong Kong: Chasing the Virus,” which aired in June 2003, reporter and producer Renata Simone went inside an earlier outbreak of a coronavirus that also originated in mainland China: SARS. It spread to the rest of the world after a man from China’s Guangdong province attended a wedding in Hong Kong and unknowingly infected nine other guests at the hotel where he was staying.

As the outbreak unfolded, Simone traveled to Hong Kong. Usually a bustling hub of commerce, the port city had been brought to a virtual standstill. Adding to the fear gripping Hong Kong: There was no cure or proven treatment for SARS.

As the sense of urgency mounted, Simone filmed with an international group of researchers who were teaming up at the University of Hong Kong to try to combat SARS, following their efforts to find a cure. The team included Dr. David Ho, a world-renowned AIDS researcher based at Columbia University in New York who hoped his expertise would be transferable.

By the time the SARS epidemic ultimately wound down that same year, contained through public health measures like testing, quarantine and isolation, close to 800 people had died. 

“Hong Kong: Chasing the Virus” was reported by Renata Simone, and produced by Simone and 
Raney Aronson-Rath. The founder and executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

ABSTRACT
Programming languages are a halfway house between the metal and the mind, a bridge between the world of circuits and the world of applications, the engineered and the social. Programming languages are the medium through which developers codify systems and fragments. In each programming language is embedded a philosophy (or many) of how to think about code, how to organise thoughts, how to design. Programming languages also define skillsets, ecosystems, jobs, loyalties and communities.

When we think of software and technology we often think in terms of progress and rapid change. Programming languages, however, typically move at a far slower pace. Mainstream languages are still embracing ideas that are decades old. Constructs that developers welcome as new to their language of choice are often older than the developers themselves.
And over all this hangs the question, what of the future?
How will current trends, from FOSS to LLMs, shape programming languages and their use?

In this talk, we will take a tour of the past, present and future of programming languages. [...]

items.title: We Need To Talk About Leopold
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Taking care of your health just got easier, thanks to my sponsor Zocdoc! Start here at: https://zocdoc.com/patrickboyle

Last week, 24-year-old Leopold Aschenbrenner — former FTX staffer, ex-OpenAI researcher, and author of the viral 165-page essay "Situational Awareness" — managed to lose roughly two-thirds of his $45 billion hedge fund in a matter of weeks. The margin calls arrived during his wedding weekend.

In this video I break down how a trader with no professional experience raised billions from Silicon Valley, why his AI "hedge" wasn't a hedge at all, and how leverage plus a concentrated bet on artificial intelligence stocks turned a great-looking expected return into a catastrophic outcome. Along the way we look at the cultural gap between Silicon Valley and Wall Street, why Ken Griffin's Citadel ended up buying the collapsing portfolio in an overnight fire sale, and the maths of volatility drag — the reason a high expected return can still drag an investor's typical outcome straight into the ground.

It's a story about leverage, risk management, expected versus median returns, and what happens when you go "full Kelly." Featuring reporting from the Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and the Financial Times, plus Victor Haghani's lessons from The Missing Billionaires.

items.title: Should Sirens Have Been Activated During Maui's Wildfire?
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Three years ago today, one of the deadliest wildfires in U.S. history began in Hawaii, reducing much of the town of Lahaina to ashes. Questions remain about the chaotic response to the tragedy, including if emergency sirens should have been activated.

FRONTLINE's 2024 documentary “Maui’s Deadly Firestorm” is now streaming on our YouTube channel.</article>
